items.title: L7: Rates, productivity and unit costs
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: A rate compares one quantity with another, such as cases per hour or pounds per page. To find a rate, divide the quantity by the time or the number of units. To go the other way, multiply. Work in a single unit of time and convert before you divide: 2 hours 45 minutes is 2.75 hours, not 2.45, because 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour. Productivity is output per unit of input, so output per member of staff or per hour worked. If output rises 40% and staff rise 25%, productivity rises by 1.40 ÷ 1.25 = 1.12, which is 12%, not 15%. Unit cost is total cost divided by the number of items. When a cost has a fixed part and a variable part, the average cost per item falls as volume rises, because the fixed part is spread more widely. A print job with a £120 set-up and 8p a copy costs 8p plus £120 spread over the copies. For backlog questions, the net clearance rate is the rate you clear minus the rate new work arrives. Staff cannot work all the time, so remove breaks and training from available hours, and include wrap-up time in each task when asked. Always say what the answer is per: per person, per hour, per case. A wrong unit gives a plausible but wrong figure.

questions.prompt: A team of 8 closes 1,440 cases in 6 working days of 7.5 hours each. How many cases does each person close per hour, on average?
questions.hint: Total person-hours are 8 × 6 × 7.5 = 360, and 1,440 ÷ 360 = 4.

questions.prompt: A print job has a £120 set-up charge plus 8p a copy. What is the average cost per copy for 5,000 copies, including the set-up charge?

options.text: 8p

questions.prompt: A unit's staff numbers rise by 25% and its output rises by 40%. What is the change in output per member of staff?

options.text: A rise of 15%
A rise of 40%
A fall of 10.7%
A rise of 12%

questions.prompt: A courier delivers 18 parcels in 2 hours 15 minutes. How many parcels is that per hour?
questions.hint: 2 hours 15 minutes is 2.25 hours, and 18 ÷ 2.25 = 8.

questions.prompt: An adviser's shift is 7.5 hours, of which one hour is reserved for breaks and training. Each call takes 9 minutes plus 3 minutes of wrap-up. How many complete calls can the adviser handle?
questions.hint: 390 available minutes ÷ 12 minutes per call = 32.5, so 32 complete calls.

questions.prompt: Last year a service cost £480,000 for 6,000 cases. This year it cost £525,000 for 7,500 cases. What was the change in cost per case?

options.text: A fall of 12.5%
A rise of 25%
A rise of 9.4%
A fall of 10%

questions.hint: Cost per case went from £80 to £70, a fall of 10 ÷ 80 = 12.5%.

questions.prompt: A backlog stands at 3,600 cases. A team clears 90 cases a day, while 30 new cases arrive each day. How many days will it take to clear the backlog?
questions.hint: Net clearance is 60 a day, and 3,600 ÷ 60 = 60.

questions.prompt: A task takes 2 hours 45 minutes. What is the total time for 11 such tasks?

options.text: 31 hours 15 minutes
30 hours 45 minutes
30 hours 25 minutes
30 hours 15 minutes

questions.hint: 11 × 2.75 = 30.25 hours, which is 30 hours 15 minutes.

items.title: L7: Pay, pro rata and the cost of staff
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Pay questions turn up often because they mix percentages, fractions and time. Pro rata means in proportion: a part-time worker on three days of a five-day week earns 3/5, or 60%, of the full-time salary and gets 60% of the full-time leave. If someone also works only part of the year, apply both fractions. To convert a salary to an hourly rate, divide by the hours worked in a year: weekly hours multiplied by 52. Overtime is often paid at time and a half, which means 1.5 times the normal hourly rate for each extra hour, and only for hours above the contracted figure. Pay awards compound when applied one after another, but a single stated percentage is applied once. To find a salary before a rise, divide by the multiplier: 1.04 for a 4% rise. Tax is charged in bands, and each rate applies only to the income that falls within its band. A simple example: 0% on the first £12,000, 20% on the next £30,000, and 40% above £42,000. On £50,000 the tax is 20% of £30,000 plus 40% of £8,000, which is £9,200. These bands are illustrative. Employer on-costs, such as pensions and national insurance, are extra percentages added to salary, and they add together when both are based on salary. Check whether a deduction is taken from gross pay and whether the question asks for gross, net or total cost.

questions.prompt: A full-time salary is £32,400. How much is paid to an employee who works three days of a five-day week?
Using illustrative bands of 0% on the first £12,000, 20% on the next £30,000 and 40% above £42,000, how much tax is due on £50,000?
An employee earns £16 an hour for a 37-hour week. Hours above 37 are paid at time and a half. What is the pay for a 43-hour week?
After a 4% pay rise, a salary is £31,200. What was it before the rise?
Full-time annual leave is 28 days. A colleague works 3 days in a five-day week and will be employed for 9 months of the year. What is their leave entitlement for the year?

options.text: 16.8 days
21 days
12.6 days
15.75 days

questions.prompt: A member of staff is paid £30,000. Employer pension costs are 26% of salary and other employer costs are 10% of salary. What is the total cost of employing them?
questions.hint: The on-costs are 36% of salary, so the cost is 30,000 × 1.36.

questions.prompt: A monthly gross salary is £2,400. Tax and national insurance take 22% of gross and a pension contribution takes 5% of gross. What is the net monthly pay?
questions.hint: The deductions total 27%, leaving 73% of £2,400, which is £1,752.

questions.prompt: A salary of £37,000 is for a 37-hour week, 52 weeks a year. What is the hourly rate?

items.title: L7: Chained fractions, percentages and groups
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Some questions chain several steps, where each step works on what is left from the one before. Take them in order and write down the number after every step. A fraction of a remainder is not a fraction of the original: if 3/8 of a budget goes to staffing and 40% of what is left goes to IT, the IT share is 40% of 5/8, not 40% of the whole. A percentage of a percentage means multiplying: if 60% of staff are in the regions and 45% of those are part-time, 27% of all staff are regional part-timers. Net headcount change needs leavers, joiners and the starting figure: leavers are taken off first, then joiners added, and the percentage change is divided by the starting figure. A rise followed by an equal fall in percentage terms does not return to the start, because the second percentage is taken of a different base. A 15% rise followed by a 15% fall is 1.15 × 0.85 = 0.9775, a fall of 2.25%. When groups change at different rates, work out each group's new size, then add. Finally, compare percentage rises as well as absolute ones, because a smaller group can grow proportionally faster. State differences between percentages in percentage points.

questions.prompt: A budget of £840,000 is split so that 3/8 goes on staffing and 40% of the remainder goes on IT. How much is left after staffing and IT?
questions.hint: Staffing is £315,000, the remainder is £525,000, IT is £210,000, leaving £315,000.

questions.prompt: A department has 1,600 staff. In a year 5% leave and 120 are recruited. What is the percentage change in headcount?

options.text: A rise of 2.5%
A rise of 7.5%
A fall of 5%
A rise of 2.4%

questions.hint: Leavers are 80 so the total becomes 1,640, a rise of 40 ÷ 1,600.

questions.prompt: Of 960 candidates, 5/12 reach the sift, 30% of those are interviewed, and 1 in 4 of those interviewed are appointed. How many are appointed?
questions.hint: 960 × 5/12 = 400, then 120 interviewed, then 30 appointed.

questions.prompt: A price rises by 15% and then falls by 15%. What is the net change?

options.text: A fall of 0.225%
A rise of 2.25%
Unchanged overall
A fall of 2.25%

questions.prompt: 60% of staff work in the regions. 45% of regional staff are part-time. What percentage of all staff are regional part-timers?
In a survey of 1,250 people, 56% agree with a statement and a quarter of those who agree say they agree strongly. How many people agree strongly?
questions.hint: 1,250 × 0.56 = 700, and a quarter is 175.

questions.prompt: In 2020 applications from Region A and Region B were in the ratio 3:2, 500 in total. By 2023 A's applications rose by 20% and B's fell by 10%. What was the total in 2023?
Group X rose from 200 to 250 and group Y from 500 to 580. Which group had the larger percentage rise, and by how many percentage points?

options.text: Y, by 30 percentage points
X, by 9 percentage points
X, by 25 percentage points
Y, by 9 percentage points

questions.hint: X rose 25% and Y rose 16%, a gap of 9 points, even though Y added more people.

items.title: L7: Budgets, variances and forecasts
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Finance questions give budgets and actual spend and ask what has happened or what will happen. A variance is actual minus budget, and it is usually shown with its direction: overspend where actual is higher than budget, underspend where it is lower. A percentage variance is the variance divided by the budget. When several lines are given, add the variances first, because overspends and underspends offset each other, then divide by the total budget. A run-rate forecast assumes spending continues at the same monthly pace: spend to date divided by months elapsed, then multiplied by 12. If the rate is not even across the year, a simple run rate can mislead. Contingency is a reserve added as a percentage of base cost, and tax is often added on top of the cost including contingency, so apply them one after the other. Savings per unit are multiplied by volume and by the number of periods. Break-even volume is the fixed cost divided by the contribution each unit makes: price minus variable cost. Per-head figures need the headcount as well as the cost. Inflation compounds, so a 4% annual rise over three years multiplies by 1.04 three times, which is about 12.5% rather than 12%. Read what the question wants: forecast outturn, variance, or percentage, and keep the sign.

questions.prompt: A budget is £360,000. £288,000 was spent in the first 9 months at a steady rate. As a percentage of the budget, what is the forecast overspend for the year?
questions.hint: The run rate gives £384,000 for the year, so £24,000 over, and 24,000 ÷ 360,000 is about 6.7%.

questions.prompt: Line A: budget £50,000, actual £54,000. Line B: budget £80,000, actual £76,000. Line C: budget £20,000, actual £21,500. What is the overall variance as a percentage of the total budget?

options.text: 1.0% underspend
1.0% overspend
5.0% overspend
3.5% overspend

questions.prompt: A project costs £2,500,000 before contingency. Contingency is 12% of the base cost, and 20% VAT is then added to the total including contingency. What is the final cost?
A unit has a £1,200,000 budget for 40 staff. The budget rises by 10% and staff increase to 50. What is the change in budget per member of staff?

options.text: A rise of 10%
A fall of 20%
A fall of 12%
A fall of 10%

questions.hint: Budget per head goes from £30,000 to £1,320,000 ÷ 50 = £26,400.

questions.prompt: A new process saves 18 minutes on each of 2,000 cases a month. Staff time is valued at £24 an hour. What is the annual saving?
Spending in four quarters was £120,000, £150,000, £135,000 and £195,000. The annual budget is £600,000. What percentage of the budget had been spent by the end of the third quarter?
questions.hint: Cumulative spend is £405,000, and 405 ÷ 600 = 0.675.

questions.prompt: An event has fixed costs of £9,000. Each ticket sells for £30 and costs £12 to provide. How many tickets must be sold to break even?
questions.hint: Each ticket contributes £18, and 9,000 ÷ 18 = 500.

questions.prompt: An item costs £2,000 today and prices rise by 4% a year. What will it cost in three years if prices keep rising at that rate?

items.title: L7: Likelihood, counting and sampling
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Some numerical tests include probability and counting. Probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the number of equally likely outcomes. If 45 of 120 applicants are shortlisted, the chance a random applicant is shortlisted is 45/120, or 3/8, and the chance they are not is 5/8. For independent events, multiply: if two checks catch 80% and 75% of errors independently, the chance an error escapes both is 0.2 × 0.25 = 0.05, so 95% are caught by at least one. 'At least one' is usually easiest as 1 minus 'none'. Counting methods depend on order. Arranging 4 different people in a queue gives 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 orders. Choosing a chair and a secretary from 5 gives 5 × 4 = 20, because the roles differ, but choosing a panel of 3 from 6 gives 20 because order does not matter: 6 × 5 × 4 ÷ (3 × 2 × 1). Expected numbers are probability multiplied by the total. A sample's proportion estimates the proportion in the full group: 14 errors in a random sample of 200 suggests 7% overall, so about 840 errors in 12,000 claims. Conditional probability restricts the group first: the chance a randomly chosen manager works in London is managers in London divided by all managers, not by all London staff.

questions.prompt: 120 applicants apply, and 45 are shortlisted. One name is picked at random. What is the probability that this applicant was not shortlisted?
questions.hint: 75 out of 120 were not shortlisted, which is 5/8.

questions.prompt: One check catches 80% of errors and a second independent check catches 75%. What percentage of errors are caught by at least one check?
questions.hint: The chance both miss an error is 0.2 × 0.25 = 0.05.

questions.prompt: A panel of 3 is chosen from 6 eligible staff. Order does not matter. How many different panels are possible?
A chair and a secretary are to be chosen from 5 colleagues, and no one can hold both roles. How many different pairings are possible?
questions.hint: 5 choices for chair and 4 for secretary gives 20.

questions.prompt: 3% of 8,000 forms contain an error, and 2 in 5 of those errors are serious. How many serious errors would you expect?
A fair spinner has five equal sectors numbered 1 to 5 and is spun twice. What is the probability that the two numbers add to 10?
questions.hint: Only 5 and 5 gives 10, so 1/5 × 1/5.

questions.prompt: In a random sample of 200 claims, 14 contain errors. Estimate the number of claims with errors in a population of 12,000.
A department has 60 staff, of whom 36 work in London. 15 London staff and 9 staff elsewhere are managers. A manager is chosen at random. What is the probability that the manager works in London?
questions.hint: 15 of the 24 managers work in London, which is 5/8.

items.title: L7: Verdicts in longer policy and report passages
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: At this level the passages are longer and the statements depend on combining two or three facts. Method: read the passage once for sense, then read again and write a one-line note for each sentence, marking every number, qualifier and exception. Break the statement into its parts and find the evidence for each. If every part is supported the verdict is True; if any part is contradicted it is False; if all parts are consistent but one part is not covered it is Cannot say. Avoid supplying missing facts from general knowledge. For example, if a policy exempts secondments 'of up to two years' from advertising and the passage says seven posts were filled by secondment, you do not know that all seven were within two years, so you cannot say none needed an exception. Treat fractions and percentages carefully. A third of 30% is exactly 10%, so a claim of 'more than 10%' is false. 'At least two thirds' includes exactly two thirds. Be careful with maximums: 'up to 10% of turnover' sets a ceiling of £500,000 on a £5m turnover. Where a condition for a future decision refers to a second trial, a result from the first trial does not satisfy it. Finally, remember that a rule shows what is required, not what actually happened.

questions.prompt: "The department's recruitment policy requires every vacancy at grade 7 and above to be advertised externally, unless it is a secondment of up to two years or has been agreed as an exception by the HR director. Last year 18 posts at grade 7 were filled. Eleven were advertised externally and the rest were secondments." Statement: "None of the grade 7 posts filled last year needed an exception from the HR director." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the number of posts advertised externally is not given
True: the seven other posts were secondments, which are exempt
False: seven posts were not advertised externally
Cannot say: the length of the secondments is not given

questions.hint: Only secondments of up to two years are exempt, and the length is not given.

questions.prompt: "An inspection of 60 care homes found that 45 met every standard. Of the 15 that did not, 10 had been inspected the previous year and had met every standard then." Statement: "At least two thirds of the homes that failed a standard this year had met every standard a year earlier." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: 10 out of 15 is exactly two thirds
False: only a quarter of the homes failed a standard
Cannot say: it is not known whether the other five were inspected
Cannot say: the passage does not say whether failed homes will be re-inspected

questions.hint: 'At least' includes exactly two thirds.

questions.prompt: "Pass rates in a licensing exam rose from 58% in 2022 to 66% in 2023. The number of candidates also rose, from 2,400 to 3,000." Statement: "More candidates passed the exam in 2023 than in 2022." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: pass rates can rise while the number passing falls
Cannot say: the number of candidates is not the number of passes
True: 66% of 3,000 is 1,980, compared with 1,392 in 2022
Cannot say: the exam may have been made easier in 2023

questions.prompt: "A permit may be issued to anyone who has lived in the area for five years. It lasts three years and may be renewed once for a further three years if the holder still lives in the area. One holder's permit was first issued in 2019." Statement: "This holder's permit could still be valid in 2026." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: it is not known if the holder still lives there
False: it runs out in 2022, or 2025 at the latest with one renewal
Cannot say: the month the permit was issued is not given
True: permits can be renewed while the holder lives in the area

questions.hint: Two periods of three years from 2019 end by 2025.

questions.prompt: "In a department, 70% of staff are below grade 7. Of the staff at grade 7 and above, a third work in London." Statement: "More than 10% of the department's staff are at grade 7 or above and work in London." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the number of staff is not given
Cannot say: lower grades in London are not mentioned
True: a third of the senior staff is a large share
False: a third of the 30% at grade 7 and above is exactly 10%

questions.hint: One third of 30% is 10%, which is not more than 10%.

questions.prompt: "A trial of a reminder text reduced missed appointments from 14% to 11% among 5,000 patients. Each text cost 4p to send." Statement: "The reminders saved the service money overall." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the cost of a missed appointment is not given
Cannot say: the passage does not say how long the trial lasted
True: fewer appointments were missed
False: sending 5,000 texts costs money

questions.hint: Saving depends on comparing the cost of texts with the cost of missed appointments.

questions.prompt: "The regulator may fine a company up to 10% of its annual turnover for a serious breach. It must allow 28 days for a response before issuing a fine." Statement: "A company with a turnover of £5m could be fined £600,000 for a serious breach." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say how serious the breach is
Cannot say: the 28-day period may have ended
False: the most it could be fined is 10% of £5m, which is £500,000
True: the regulator may fine up to a given percentage

questions.hint: The limit is a ceiling of £500,000.

questions.prompt: "A pilot cut the average time to process a licence application from 30 working days to 24. The department will extend the pilot nationally if the average falls below 25 working days in a second pilot region." Statement: "The pilot's result has already met the department's condition for national extension." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: 24 days is below 25 days
Cannot say: the condition refers to a second region's result
Cannot say: the number of applications is not given
False: the pilot has not yet been extended nationally

questions.hint: The result needed is from the second region, not the first.

items.title: L7: Verdicts that turn on hedging words
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Small words change the meaning of a statement, and verbal tests exploit them. 'Usually', 'often' and 'generally' allow exceptions, so a statement that says 'always' or 'every' goes beyond them. 'May' is permission or possibility, 'should' is advice or a target, and 'must' is an obligation. A response that misses a 'should' target but meets the 'must' limit has not broken the requirement. 'Up to' sets a ceiling, not a typical figure. 'At least' sets a floor. 'Most' means more than half, while 'fewer than 50 out of 400' lets you say that more than 350 are not in that group. 'Only' and 'unless' set conditions: a rule that says 'only managers who have completed the programme may apply' says who is allowed, not who did. 'Unless a manager objects' removes the permission if an objection is made. Partial evidence also matters: if only some sites reported results, you cannot say what happened across all of them. Words such as 'partly' or 'in part' signal that a claim has caveats, so a statement that ignores them may go beyond the text. Worked example: a passage says staff 'should reply within five days and must reply within ten'. A reply on day eight misses the target but is still within the obligation. Check the exact verb before you pick a verdict.

questions.prompt: "Complaints are usually answered within ten working days. Complex complaints may take up to thirty working days." Statement: "Every complaint is answered within thirty working days." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say what makes a complaint complex
False: most complaints are answered within ten days
Cannot say: 'usually' allows ordinary complaints to take longer than ten days
True: complex complaints are capped at thirty days, so none take longer

questions.hint: The thirty-day ceiling is given only for complex complaints.

questions.prompt: "Most of the 400 people at the event were civil servants. Fewer than 50 attendees were from local government." Statement: "More than 300 attendees were not from local government." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: other groups may have attended
True: fewer than 50 were from local government, so more than 350 were not
Cannot say: the number of civil servants is not given
False: most attendees were civil servants, not local government staff

questions.hint: 400 minus fewer than 50 leaves more than 350.

questions.prompt: "Only managers who have completed the leadership programme may apply for the senior post. Applications closed on Friday, and 12 managers applied." Statement: "All 12 applicants had completed the leadership programme." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: only managers who completed it may apply
False: some applicants may be disqualified
Cannot say: the number of places is not given
Cannot say: the passage states who may apply, not who actually applied

questions.hint: A rule does not prove that it was followed.

questions.prompt: "The agency should respond to requests within five days and must respond within ten." Statement: "A response sent after eight days breaches the agency's obligation." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: the binding limit is ten days, so day eight misses only a target
True: any response after five days is late
Cannot say: the type of request is not given
Cannot say: the passage does not say what happens after ten days

questions.hint: 'Should' sets a target and 'must' sets the obligation.

questions.prompt: "Over a decade the proportion of claims decided in the claimant's favour rose from 31% to 44%. Officials caution that the rise is partly due to a change in how claims are recorded." Statement: "The tribunal is now more favourable to claimants than it was a decade ago." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: the proportion decided for claimants has risen
False: officials say the figures are unreliable
Cannot say: part of the rise may come from the change in recording
Cannot say: the passage does not say how many claims were made in total

questions.hint: 'Partly' means the rise cannot be taken at face value.

questions.prompt: "Not all of the pilot's sites reported results. Of the 20 that did, 14 showed shorter waiting times." Statement: "Waiting times fell at most of the pilot's sites." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: some sites did not report any change
Cannot say: the number of sites that did not report is unknown
Cannot say: the passage does not say how long the pilot lasted
True: 14 out of 20 is 70%

questions.hint: If more than 28 sites ran the pilot, 14 would not be a majority.

questions.prompt: "A review recommended that, wherever possible, interviews be held in person. The department has accepted all the review's recommendations." Statement: "All interviews in the department will now be held in person." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: 'wherever possible' allows exceptions
False: some interviews will be held online
True: the department has accepted the recommendation
Cannot say: the review's findings are not described

questions.hint: The recommendation is qualified, so the passage does not support 'all'.

questions.prompt: "Unless a manager objects, staff may carry over up to five days of leave to the next year. Nia's manager has objected to any carry-over for her team." Statement: "Nia can carry over five days of leave." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say why the manager objected
Cannot say: the passage does not say that Nia is in the team
True: staff may carry over up to five days
False: the manager's objection removes the permission to carry over leave

questions.hint: 'Unless' makes the permission conditional on there being no objection.

items.title: L7: Necessary and sufficient conditions
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Many logic questions turn on the difference between a necessary condition and a sufficient one. A condition is necessary if the outcome cannot happen without it: 'a grant is awarded only if the project is on the priority list' makes being on the list necessary, so if a grant was awarded the project must be on the list. A condition is sufficient if it guarantees the outcome: 'staff who complete the course and have it signed off receive the bonus' makes both together sufficient. If someone did not receive the bonus, they did not meet both conditions, but you cannot say which one they missed. Take care with 'both … and': two requirements are each necessary. 'Either … or' means one of the conditions is enough. A frequent trap is affirming the consequent: from 'if the system is down, use the paper form' and 'staff used the paper form' you cannot conclude the system was down. Another is denying the antecedent: from 'if the report is late the minister is told' and 'the report was on time' you cannot conclude the minister was not told. Test an option by asking whether it must be true in every situation consistent with the passage. If you can imagine a consistent situation where it fails, it does not follow.

questions.prompt: To be appointed, a candidate must pass the interview and the security check. Some candidates who pass the interview fail the security check. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Passing the interview guarantees appointment
Some candidates who pass the interview are not appointed
Everyone who passes the security check is appointed
A candidate who fails the interview may still be appointed

questions.hint: The security check is also necessary, so passing the interview is not enough.

questions.prompt: A grant is awarded only if the project is on the priority list. The Hillside project was awarded a grant. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Hillside would have been awarded a grant under any conditions
Every project on the priority list receives a grant
The Hillside project is on the priority list
Hillside was the only project awarded a grant

questions.hint: Being on the list is necessary for an award.

questions.prompt: Staff receive the bonus if they complete the course and their manager signs it off. Dee did not receive the bonus. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Dee did not complete the course at all
Only staff with a sign-off can ever receive the bonus
Dee's manager refused to sign the course off
Dee did not both complete the course and have it signed off

questions.hint: Both conditions together are sufficient, so Dee missed at least one.

questions.prompt: Access to the archive requires both a pass and an escort. Lin has a pass. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Lin can enter the archive only if she also has an escort
Lin has an escort
Lin cannot enter the archive
Lin can enter the archive

questions.hint: The pass is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.prompt: All claims over £10,000 are reviewed by a panel, and only senior officers can sit on the panel. A £12,000 claim was submitted. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Claims under £10,000 are never seen by senior officers
A senior officer was involved in reviewing the claim
The panel approved the claim
Claims reviewed by senior officers are always over £10,000

questions.hint: The claim must go to a panel, and only senior officers sit on it.

questions.prompt: If the system is down, staff must use the paper form. Staff used the paper form on Tuesday. What can be concluded?

options.text: The paper form is only used on Tuesdays
The system was working but staff chose paper
Nothing definite about whether the system was down
The system was down on Tuesday

questions.hint: Staff might use the paper form for other reasons.

questions.prompt: A visitor is admitted only if a member of staff vouches for them or they hold a valid pass. Kay holds no valid pass and was admitted. Which statement must be true?

options.text: A member of staff vouched for Kay
Kay was admitted in error
All visitors need a staff member to vouch for them
Kay is a member of staff

questions.hint: With no pass, the other alternative must apply.

questions.prompt: The audit will be extended if more than five errors are found in the sample, or if any single error exceeds £1,000. Four errors were found and the largest was £1,200. Which statement must be true?

options.text: The audit will be extended only if more than five errors are found
Nothing can be said about extending the audit
The audit will not be extended because only four errors were found
The audit will be extended

questions.hint: One error over £1,000 is enough on its own.

items.title: L7: Main conclusions, evidence and counter-claims
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Before you can judge an argument you must see its structure. The main conclusion is the point the author wants you to accept. Evidence or premises support it. Some arguments have an intermediate conclusion, which is supported by earlier statements and in turn supports the main conclusion. Words such as 'therefore', 'so', 'hence' and 'it follows that' often introduce a conclusion, while 'because', 'since' and 'given that' introduce support. Some passages also include a counter-claim, a view the author mentions in order to answer it. A statement that begins 'Some argue that…' is usually a position being examined, not the author's own view. Background information sets the scene but does not support the conclusion. Method: first, find the question the argument answers. Second, pick the statement that the others are there to support. Third, check that your choice is something the author recommends or claims, not just a fact. Worked example: 'Some argue that the scheme should be scrapped because it costs £2m a year. But it supports 3,000 jobs. Therefore the scheme should continue.' The main conclusion is that the scheme should continue. The cost is the counter-claim's evidence, and the 3,000 jobs are the author's evidence.

questions.prompt: "Some argue that the scheme should be scrapped because it costs £2m a year. But it supports 3,000 jobs. Therefore the scheme should continue." What is the main conclusion?

options.text: The scheme should be scrapped
The scheme supports 3,000 jobs
The scheme costs £2m a year
The scheme should continue

questions.hint: 'Therefore' introduces the author's conclusion.

questions.prompt: "Staff turnover in the unit is high. High turnover is costly because new staff must be trained. The unit should therefore review why staff leave." What is the main conclusion?

options.text: The unit should review why staff leave
New staff must be trained before they are productive
High turnover is costly for the unit
Staff turnover in the unit is currently high

questions.hint: The recommendation is what the other statements support.

questions.prompt: A unit manager argues that turnover is costly because of training needs, and so a review of leavers is justified. What role does the claim that turnover is costly play?

options.text: It is the main conclusion of the whole passage
It is a counter-claim the author rejects
It is an intermediate conclusion that supports the recommendation
It is background that does not support anything

questions.hint: It is supported by the training point and in turn supports the recommendation.

questions.prompt: "The report was published late. The author says a data error caused the delay. Yet the error was found two weeks before the deadline, which left time to fix it. So the delay cannot have been caused only by the data error." What is the main conclusion?

options.text: The data error was found two weeks before the deadline arrived
The delay cannot have been caused only by the data error
The author's explanation is the only possible one
The report was published later than planned

questions.hint: 'So' marks the author's own conclusion.

questions.prompt: "Cities with more cycle lanes have lower pollution. Some say the lanes reduce car use. But most lanes were built in cities that already had less traffic. So the figures do not show that lanes reduce pollution." What role does "Some say the lanes reduce car use" play?

options.text: It is the author's main conclusion
It is evidence for the author's conclusion
It is a view that the author goes on to challenge
It is background that is not connected to the argument

questions.hint: The 'But' signals that the author rejects the claim.

questions.prompt: "Although the new system is expensive, it is reliable and staff like it, so it is worth the cost." What is the main conclusion?

options.text: The new system is expensive to buy and run
Staff like the new system a great deal
The new system is reliable in everyday use
The new system is worth the cost

questions.hint: 'So' introduces the conclusion; the rest is the case for it.

questions.prompt: "Because the contract was awarded without competition, the department breached its procurement rules." Which statement is the evidence?

options.text: The contract was awarded without competition
The contract was awarded by the department
The department breached its procurement rules
The department has procurement rules

questions.hint: 'Because' introduces the support for the claim.

questions.prompt: "We cannot hire more staff this year. Because of this we must prioritise. So the helpline backlog should be cleared first, since complaints rise when callers wait." What is the final conclusion?

options.text: Complaints rise when callers have to wait
The helpline backlog should be cleared first
We cannot hire any more staff this year
We must prioritise what we do this year

questions.hint: Prioritising is a step towards the final recommendation.

items.title: L7: Explaining puzzling results
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Some verbal questions describe two facts that seem to conflict and ask which additional fact best explains both. The right answer reconciles the facts without contradicting either, and it works in the specific case rather than in general. Method: restate the puzzle as a question, such as 'How can applications fall while approvals rise?'. Then think about what kinds of change could produce both results at once. Typical resolutions are a change in composition (who is counted), a change in definition or measurement, a time lag, or two different groups moving in different directions. Test each option by asking whether, if it were true, both facts would be expected. Reject options that explain only one fact, that repeat the puzzle, or that bring in an unrelated detail. Worked example: the average salary in a unit rose by 8% yet no individual's pay changed. This is explained by lower-paid staff leaving or higher-paid staff joining, so the mix changed. 'Staff were pleased with their jobs' explains nothing about the average. Averages and proportions are particularly sensitive to changes in who is in the group, so look for composition effects when you see them.

questions.prompt: After a new online form was introduced, applications fell by 20% but approvals rose by 5%. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: The form screens out ineligible applicants before they can submit
More people heard about the scheme in the local press that month
The form is easier to use than the old paper one
Approvals take longer to process than applications do

questions.hint: Fewer, better-targeted applications could produce more approvals.

questions.prompt: A call centre's average call length fell by two minutes, but total staff hours spent on calls rose. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: Staff were given extra training on call handling that year
Staff took longer breaks between their calls
Calls were answered more quickly than before
The number of calls rose by more than the call length fell

questions.hint: More calls, even if shorter, can use more total hours.

questions.prompt: A department's spending on training fell by 15% but staff reported more hours of training. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: The department employed more staff during the year than before
The department moved much training to cheaper online modules
Staff said they valued training very highly
Training budgets were cut across all government departments

questions.hint: Cheaper formats allow more hours for less money.

questions.prompt: The proportion of staff in senior grades rose even though no one was promoted. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: Senior staff received a pay rise during the year
The department introduced a new promotion scheme
A large number of staff in junior grades left during the year
Several senior staff moved to other departments that year

questions.hint: Fewer junior staff raises the senior share without any promotion.

questions.prompt: An inspectorate found more breaches under its new regime than under the old one, yet it says compliance improved. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: The penalties for breaches were increased under the new regime
The new regime inspects far more premises, and the share in breach fell
Businesses disliked the new regime and said so
Inspectors were given more training under the new regime

questions.hint: A higher count can coexist with a lower rate when coverage grows.

questions.prompt: The average salary in a unit rose by 8% although nobody's pay changed. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: The unit moved to a new building in the summer
Staff kept the same working hours as they had before
Several low-paid staff left and higher-paid staff joined
Staff morale improved a good deal during the year

questions.hint: The mix of staff changed, which changes the average.

questions.prompt: More people used a helpline last year, but complaints about the helpline fell. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: The complaints procedure is rarely used by the public
Many callers were using the helpline for the first time
The helpline is now open for longer hours
A new online booking option removed the long call queues

questions.hint: Better service quality can reduce complaints even as use grows.

questions.prompt: A town's recorded crime fell by 10%, but surveys show more residents say they fear crime. Which fact best explains this?

options.text: High-profile local incidents received heavy media coverage
The survey was carried out in the autumn months
The police force was reorganised during that year
Crime is lower in the town than the national average

questions.hint: Perceptions can move independently of recorded figures.

items.title: L7: Managing performance and difficult conversations
items.source: Civil Service Code and Civil Service performance management guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: As an experienced EO you may supervise junior colleagues, and the Civil Service Code expects you to act with integrity and objectivity and to treat people with fairness and respect. Good management of performance is early, specific and fair. When a team member's work falls short, you should talk to them promptly rather than waiting for a formal review, describe the specific behaviour or outcome with examples, listen to their account, check whether something is getting in the way, such as workload, unclear instructions, health or a personal difficulty, and agree clear steps and a date to review progress. Keep a factual note of what was said and agreed. Where there may be an underlying health or caring issue, involve your own line manager or HR for advice, and use the department's policies. You should not discuss one person's performance with the wider team, compare them publicly, or label them as lazy. Equally, you should not ignore problems to avoid conflict, because that is unfair to the person, to colleagues who carry extra work and to the public. Praise good work in the same specific way. Worked example: a colleague has missed three deadlines. You hold a private conversation soon after the latest one, set out the dates, ask what is happening, agree support and a review date, and record it. Avoid vague criticism, public embarrassment, or silent resentment.

questions.prompt: A colleague you supervise has missed three deadlines this month. What is the most effective first step?

options.text: Speak to them privately soon, set out the dates and agree support
Ask the team in a meeting why work is slipping
Quietly give their tasks to other team members to protect deadlines
Wait for the end-of-year review so there is more evidence to discuss

questions.hint: An early, private and specific conversation is fair and gives the person a chance to improve.

questions.prompt: During a one-to-one, a team member tells you they are struggling with a family illness, which has affected their work. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell the rest of the team so they can be more understanding
Say you understand and carry on with the usual targets
Listen, explain what support is available, and involve HR for advice
Suggest they use annual leave and hand over their casework

questions.hint: Support should be offered through the proper policies, with confidentiality respected.

questions.prompt: A team member's work contains repeated errors. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Agree extra guidance and set a date to review progress
Point out the errors in front of the team so that everyone learns from them
Note down what was discussed and the support that was agreed
Show them examples of the errors and discuss their likely cause

questions.hint: Public criticism is unfair and rarely improves performance.

questions.prompt: You are asked to give feedback to a colleague who does good work but is often curt with customers. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Pair them with a colleague and not mention the real reason
Say they need to be friendlier and leave them to work out how
Wait until a customer complains formally and then raise it
Give specific examples, explain the effect on customers, and agree changes

questions.hint: Specific, timely feedback gives a person something they can act on.

questions.prompt: After you raised a concern about poor performance, the colleague says you are being unfair. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask other colleagues whether they agree with your view
Tell them it is not up for debate and end the meeting
Listen, check the facts again, and explain the examples and support on offer
Reassure them you will not mention it again to avoid conflict

questions.hint: Hearing the other side and revisiting the facts keeps the process fair.

questions.prompt: A highly capable colleague regularly finishes work late, but others cover for them. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Reduce their workload without explaining why
Tell others to stop covering and see what happens
Let others continue to cover, since the work is good quality
Address it with the colleague directly and agree changes

questions.hint: Covering for someone avoids dealing with the problem and is unfair to others.

questions.prompt: You discover that a team member has been recording incorrect times on their case records to appear faster. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Check the facts and speak to them privately about the records
Correct the records yourself and say nothing so the matter does not escalate
Make a note of what you found and the dates involved
Tell your line manager what you found and follow the policy

questions.hint: Inaccurate records are a matter of integrity and must be dealt with openly.

questions.prompt: A new starter on your team is performing below expectations after two months. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Check training and support are adequate, and agree a plan and review date
Give them easier work for a while and not tell them why
Wait to see if they improve before saying anything to them
Tell them their probation is at risk without giving any examples

questions.hint: Early review of support and expectations is fair and effective.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to delay recording their poor performance, saying they will improve. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Agree a short period of support with a review date, and keep a note
Record the problem formally but not tell them about it
Refuse any discussion and escalate straight to HR
Delay all records and rely on trust that things will get better

questions.hint: Support and accurate records can go together.

items.title: L7: Equality, fair treatment and reasonable adjustments
items.source: Equality Act 2010 and Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination because of nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Direct discrimination means treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic. Indirect discrimination arises when a rule that applies to everyone puts people with a characteristic at a disadvantage and cannot be justified. Harassment is unwanted conduct related to a characteristic that creates an intimidating or offensive environment. Employers must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, such as changing equipment, hours or procedures, so they are not placed at a substantial disadvantage. The Civil Service Code requires you to treat people with fairness and respect, and civil service recruitment is based on merit through fair and open competition. If you witness or receive a complaint of discrimination or harassment, you should take it seriously, listen, avoid judging, record the facts, and follow the department's procedure, usually involving your manager or HR. Jokes and banter that single out characteristics are not harmless just because the person laughs along. Worked example: a disabled candidate asks for extra time in a test. You do not question whether they are really disabled, you pass the request to the right team promptly, and you make sure it is handled in the same way for any candidate with a similar need.

questions.prompt: A candidate with dyslexia asks for extra time in a written test. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask for medical proof before you even pass the request on
Give the extra time but mark the test more strictly
Refuse, as extra time would be unfair to the other candidates
Pass the request promptly to the team that arranges adjustments

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty and keep the assessment fair.

questions.prompt: A colleague regularly makes jokes about another team member's accent, and the team laughs along. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ignore it, since the person being joked about also laughs along
Join in lightly so that you are not seen as being awkward
Tell the colleague privately that this is unacceptable, and report it if it continues
Ask the whole team to vote on whether the jokes are acceptable

questions.hint: Remarks related to a characteristic can amount to harassment even when no one objects aloud.

questions.prompt: A member of staff tells you in confidence that a manager made comments about her pregnancy, and she asks you to say nothing. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Report it to the manager's own line manager without telling her
Listen, explain you cannot promise silence, and encourage her to report it
Tell her to ignore the comments, as pregnancy is a sensitive topic
Promise to keep it secret and speak to the manager informally

questions.hint: Serious complaints need to be dealt with through the proper procedure.

questions.prompt: You are scoring job applications and notice that one is from a person you know to be pregnant. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Score on the evidence against the criteria only
Apply the same marking scheme to all candidates
Mark them down, as they may soon be on maternity leave
Record your reasons for each score

questions.hint: Treating pregnancy as a reason to reject is direct discrimination.

questions.prompt: A team meeting is always held on Friday afternoons, which some staff cannot attend because of religious observance. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Look at moving the meeting or finding another way for those colleagues to take part
Keep the meeting, since it was set for everyone
Tell affected staff to catch up from the minutes alone
Move the meeting to Monday without consulting anybody

questions.hint: A rule that disadvantages a group should be reviewed unless it can be justified.

questions.prompt: A disabled colleague asks to work from home two days a week because of their condition. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask them to prove their condition with a doctor's letter first
Consider the request as a reasonable adjustment and take advice from HR
Agree informally without recording or telling HR
Reject it because others would then ask for the same

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments are considered individually and recorded.

questions.prompt: You overhear a colleague say a job candidate is too old to learn the new systems. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Agree that the candidate may struggle, but keep it from the panel
Tell the candidate what was said after the interview
Say nothing, since the candidate was not present
Challenge the remark, remind them selection is on merit, and tell the panel chair

questions.hint: Age is protected, and decisions must rest on evidence about the job.

questions.prompt: A member of the public asks for a service to be delivered by a particular member of staff because of the person's gender. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Agree, since it keeps the member of the public happy with the service
Refuse and end the contact immediately without explaining
Explain that the service is provided by whoever is available
Ask them to explain their reasons in a formal letter

questions.hint: Services are provided fairly, but genuine needs should be considered.

questions.prompt: Two equally qualified internal candidates apply for a promotion. One of them is a close friend. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Sit on the panel and score both carefully, because you are sure you can be fair
Declare the friendship and follow the recruitment policy in full
Tell the chair and ask to be replaced on the interview panel
Let the other panel members score the candidates without you

questions.hint: A close friendship creates a perceived bias that must be declared.

items.title: L7: Openness, records and freedom of information
items.source: Freedom of Information Act 2000 and Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: The Freedom of Information Act 2000 gives anyone the right to ask a public authority for recorded information, and the authority must usually reply within 20 working days. A request does not have to mention the Act, but it must be in writing, give a name and an address for reply and describe the information wanted. Authorities have a duty to advise and assist requesters. Some information is exempt, for example where releasing it would prejudice the prevention of crime, or where it is personal data about someone else, but many exemptions are subject to a public interest test, and the decision is made by the people in the department with that expertise. Requests for environmental information are handled under the Environmental Information Regulations 2004. It is a criminal offence to alter, hide or destroy records after a request has been made in order to prevent their disclosure. Civil servants must also keep accurate records and must not withhold information from ministers, Parliament or the public except as authorised. The Civil Service Code requires you to be honest and open. Worked example: a colleague receives an email request for meeting notes on a policy and says it is not a proper request because it did not mention the Act. The right response is to pass it to the FOI team, since it counts as a request, and not to delete anything. Do not answer on your own if you do not have the authority to release information.

questions.prompt: You receive an email from a member of the public asking for the notes of a policy meeting, but it does not mention the Freedom of Information Act. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ignore it, since it is not a formal request
Send the notes straight away without checking them with anyone
Reply that it is not a proper request, as it does not cite the Act
Treat it as a possible FOI request and pass it to the FOI team promptly

questions.hint: A request does not need to cite the Act to count as one.

questions.prompt: A colleague suggests deleting some embarrassing emails now that an FOI request has been received for them. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Agree to delete only the emails that are clearly personal
Say that the records must be kept, and tell your manager if the colleague insists
Delete them from the system but keep a copy in case they are needed later
Say nothing, as it is the colleague's own decision to make

questions.hint: Destroying records after a request to prevent disclosure is a criminal offence.

questions.prompt: An FOI request is for information held by another team in your department. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Reply with the information, based on what you remember of it
Tell the requester to contact the other team directly instead
Hold the request until you have asked the other team informally
Pass the request to the FOI team to coordinate with the holding team

questions.hint: Requests are logged and handled centrally within the time limit.

questions.prompt: You are preparing a response and think part of the information is sensitive. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Ask the FOI team to consider whether any exemption applies to the pages
Remove the sensitive pages without telling the requester or the FOI team
Provide the full set of material to the people who decide
Flag the pages to the FOI team and explain your concern about them

questions.hint: Withholding material without proper decision-making breaches the duty to be open.

questions.prompt: A journalist asks you directly for figures that are not yet published. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Refer them to the press office, and tell the FOI team if it is a formal request
Say that the figures do not exist yet
Give the figures informally if they do not seem sensitive
Offer to share them if the journalist promises not to quote you

questions.hint: The press office and the FOI team have the authority to decide.

questions.prompt: A requester asks for information in a particular format, such as a spreadsheet. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Provide a paper copy only, because this is simpler for the team
Tell the requester to extract the data themselves from the report
Work with the FOI team to provide a usable form where practicable
Refuse because the format is not specified in the Act

questions.hint: The duty to advise and assist includes helping people to use the information.

questions.prompt: The 20-working-day deadline for an FOI response is two days away and the information is still being gathered. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Send a partial reply to the requester with no explanation
Ask the requester to withdraw the request to save time
Wait until the deadline has passed, then apologise
Tell the FOI team now so the deadline can be managed

questions.hint: Delays should be raised early so that the team can act and communicate.

questions.prompt: You are asked to keep a record of a verbal decision made at a meeting. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Keep your notes at home so that they stay private
Write a clear and accurate note promptly and store it where it can be found
Rely on your memory in case anyone asks later
Record only the decisions that are straightforward and clear

questions.hint: Accurate records are a core part of openness and accountability.

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes to hold a sensitive discussion by personal messaging app so that it is not recorded. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Explain that official business should be on official systems
Raise the matter with your manager if the colleague insists
Go along with it, as it is only an informal chat
Suggest using a meeting with a recorded note

questions.hint: Avoiding the record system to avoid scrutiny undermines openness.

items.title: L7: Spending public money properly
items.source: Managing Public Money and Civil Service Code, GOV.UK
items.body: Civil servants spend money that belongs to the public, and HM Treasury's Managing Public Money sets out the principles. Spending must be regular, which means it has the proper authority and follows the law; proper, which means it meets high standards of probity; and good value for money, which means a sensible balance of cost, quality and benefit. The senior official responsible for a body's finances is the accounting officer, who answers to Parliament. If an accounting officer is instructed by a minister to do something that appears to breach these standards, they can ask for the instruction in writing, so the matter is on record. At your level, the Civil Service Code requires you to use resources only for the authorised public purposes, to avoid waste, and to avoid creating a false impression of a supplier relationship. Procurement should be fair and open, with suppliers treated equally and decisions justified on the published criteria. Expenses should be genuine, supported by receipts and compliant with policy. Splitting a purchase into smaller parts to avoid approval limits is improper. Worked example: you are asked to spend a small remaining budget on equipment before the year ends, although it is not needed. The best response is to explain that spending must be for a genuine need and offer to raise the underspend with your manager, not to buy items just to use the money.

questions.prompt: In March, your manager asks you to spend an underspend on equipment that the team does not need. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Explain that spending must meet a genuine need, and raise the underspend with finance
Order items through several small purchases to avoid needing approval
Spend it on something for the team, to avoid losing the budget
Buy equipment that might be useful to the team in future years

questions.hint: Spending to use up money is neither proper nor good value.

questions.prompt: A purchase will cost £12,000, but you can only approve up to £10,000. A colleague suggests splitting it into two orders. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Split it into two orders, but tell your manager afterwards
Split it into two orders, since the total amount is the same
Ask the supplier to invoice in two separate months instead
Decline, and seek approval for the full amount from the right authority

questions.hint: Splitting purchases to avoid limits is improper, whatever the total.

questions.prompt: A supplier you have used before offers a lower price than competitors but is not on the approved list. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Follow the procurement rules, which may mean running or recording a competition
Delay the decision until the supplier is added to the approved list
Tell the other suppliers the price to push their offers down
Award the contract directly, since the price is so good

questions.hint: Fair and open competition is the default, with justified exceptions.

questions.prompt: You are asked to claim expenses for a train ticket you did not use. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Offer to check the policy for what can properly be claimed
Claim it, since the colleague says that everyone does this
Decline, and explain to them that claims must be genuine
Tell your manager if you are pressed to do it again

questions.hint: False expenses are fraud and cannot be justified by common practice.

questions.prompt: A minister's office asks for a payment to be made before the formal approval is complete. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Refuse and tell the minister's office to stop asking you
Make the payment early, since ministers decide priorities
Raise it with the accounting officer, who can ask for the instruction in writing
Delay the payment without saying why to anyone

questions.hint: Regularity matters, and the accounting officer has established routes for such instructions.

questions.prompt: You find that a supplier has been paid twice for the same invoice. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Report it promptly to finance so the overpayment can be recovered
Reduce the next invoice by the same amount without telling finance
Wait until the year-end reconciliation to deal with it
Keep quiet, as the supplier may notice and return it themselves

questions.hint: Public money paid in error is reported and recovered through proper processes.

questions.prompt: A colleague regularly uses the department's credit card for small personal purchases and repays them later. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Join in occasionally, as everyone else seems to do it
Ignore it, since the money is always repaid
Ask the colleague to stop and then take no further action
Raise it with your line manager or the nominated officer

questions.hint: Using public funds for personal purposes breaches the Code, even if repaid.

questions.prompt: You are asked to buy a service from a company owned by a friend of your manager, without a competition. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Agree to the purchase if the price is reasonable
Ask about the justification and say the procurement rules must be followed
Get a quote from your manager's friend and a few others
Make the purchase and keep a record of the manager's request

questions.hint: Direct awards need a proper basis, and conflicts must be managed.

questions.prompt: A team has leftover budget at the year end and a manager suggests prepaying next year's subscriptions. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Prepay, but have it invoiced as a current-year cost
Ask the supplier to hold the money until next year
Check with finance, as spending must be in the right financial year
Prepay, since the money will be spent on something useful anyway

questions.hint: Spending is controlled by financial year and must be recorded correctly.
